identification.summary: Operation Emmental is the name Trend Micro gave in 2014 to a financially motivated campaign against online-banking customers in Switzerland, Austria, Sweden and Japan, which combined a Windows DNS/certificate-hijacking Trojan with a malicious Android app to defeat SMS-based two-factor authentication [S1]. The Windows malware is known as Retefe (also Werdlod), and the same operators are called the Retefe gang [S5][S3]. Later reporting ties the macOS malware Dok to Retefe [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro linked the operators to the handles -=FreeMan=- and Northwinds, active since at least 2011 [S1]. Swiss MELANI said it knew of Retefe since November 2013 [S2]. Public reporting on Operation Emmental dates to July 2014 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: This is a cybercrime cluster, not a state-sponsored actor; Microsoft does not map it to a Typhoon, Blizzard, Sandstorm or Sleet name, and no Microsoft name is stated in the cited sources. 'Operation Emmental' is Trend Micro's campaign name; 'Retefe' is the malware family name and is used by other vendors (Proofpoint, Palo Alto Unit 42, ESET) for the same tooling [S3][S4][S7]. Whether every Retefe campaign is run by one group is not established in the cited sources.

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro stated the operators are likely Russian speakers [S1]. No state sponsor is identified in any cited source; the activity is described as bank fraud.
attribution.basis: Trend Micro linked the campaign to the handles -=FreeMan=- and Northwinds and assessed them as likely Russian speakers [S1]. No indictment or government attribution was found in the sources gathered.

objectives: Financial theft from online-banking customers by harvesting credentials and one-time passwords and redirecting bank traffic to spoofed sites [S1][S3].

regions: Switzerland (16 Swiss online banking sites reported in 2014) [S2]
Germany and Switzerland (from April 2019, Windows and macOS) [S7]
targeting.notes: Targeting is of bank customers, not banks or government networks. The Retefe command-and-control server was observed returning the proxy configuration only to hosts located in Sweden, Switzerland and Japan [S3]. The macOS Dok variant hijacked traffic only if the victim's external IP was in Switzerland [S5]. Emails were localized per country, posing as order or receipt notices from local electronics retailers [S3].

capabilities.summary: Localized phishing emails with a malicious attachment; the Windows malware changes DNS settings or sets a proxy and installs a rogue root SSL certificate so fake bank pages look trusted, then may delete itself [S1][S3]. Victims entering credentials on the fake bank site were told to install an Android app that captured SMS one-time passwords, defeating SMS-based two-factor authentication [S1]. Retefe does not use web injects; it routes bank traffic through proxy servers, often hosted on Tor [S3][S7]. Unit 42 described PowerShell being used to install the certificate and proxy configuration, and Smoke Loader being downloaded in later campaigns [S3]. In 2017 the Windows delivery used a .docx that fetched Werdlod/Retefe from a Dropbox account, alongside a zipped macOS Dok sample [S5]. Proofpoint reported EternalBlue added for internal spread in 2017 and, in 2019, a move from Tor to stunnel, Smoke Loader as intermediate loader, and abuse of a shareware app packaged as a Python script [S7]. Dok abused a signed developer certificate, installed a local certificate to enable man-in-the-middle, and used fake 'OS X update' prompts to obtain admin rights [S6].

campaigns.name: Early Retefe tracking by Swiss authorities
campaigns.summary: MELANI said authorities had known of Retefe since November 2013 and worked with Swiss banks and European partners [S2].

campaigns.name: Operation Emmental report
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro published 'Finding Holes: Operation Emmental', describing the bypass of SMS-based two-factor authentication using DNS hijacking, a rogue root certificate and a malicious Android app, with victims in Switzerland, Austria, Sweden and Japan [S1]. Swiss coverage reported 16 targeted Swiss banking sites [S2].

campaigns.name: Retefe against UK and other banks
campaigns.summary: ESET reported Retefe targeting various banks, mostly in Switzerland, Austria and the UK, including Tesco Bank [S4].

campaigns.name: OSX/Dok macOS variant
campaigns.summary: Check Point described Dok as macOS malware ported from Windows Retefe, spread by phishing (including a lure posing as a Swiss tax notice) and signed with a developer certificate Apple later revoked [S6].

campaigns.name: Combined Windows and macOS Swiss campaign
campaigns.summary: Emails carried a .docx delivering Werdlod/Retefe and a zip with a Dok sample; Trend Micro attributed the wave to the Operation Emmental actors and said Dok is the Mac version of Retefe [S5]. Proofpoint later called 2017 the last major campaign before a quiet period, noting EternalBlue added for spread [S7].

campaigns.name: Retefe resurgence against Swiss and German customers
campaigns.summary: After a mostly dormant 2018, Retefe resumed in April 2019 against Swiss and German customers on Windows and macOS, using stunnel instead of Tor and Smoke Loader as loader [S7].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated, likely Russian-speaking operators linked by Trend Micro to the handles -=FreeMan=- and Northwinds [S1].
diamond.capability: Phishing, DNS/proxy and rogue-certificate traffic hijack, Android OTP-stealing app, Retefe/Werdlod for Windows, Dok for macOS, Smoke Loader, EternalBlue spread [S1][S3][S5][S7].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker-controlled DNS servers and proxies, often on Tor, later stunnel; Dropbox used to host a payload in 2017; geo-restricted C2 [S1][S3][S5][S7].
diamond.victim: Retail online-banking customers in Switzerland, Austria, Sweden, Japan, the UK and Germany [S1][S4][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven fraud against European and Japanese banking customers; no political objective is stated in the sources [S1].
diamond.technology: Banking authentication that relies on SMS one-time passwords, user-trusted root certificate stores, and Windows and macOS endpoints that accept unsigned or abused-signed installers [S1][S6].

gaps: No state sponsor or government attribution found; the actor appears to be criminal. Relevance to DoD is indirect (personnel as consumers, financial-sector disruption).

The Trend Micro primary report (hosted copy), Proofpoint, Check Point, Unit 42 and MELANI pages could not be opened with the fetch tool; facts rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage. Re-verify against the primary documents.
Number of banks (reports of 34) and the Romania/Russia attribution wording appeared in search summaries but were not confirmed in an opened document, so they are excluded from the profile.
Source dates for the Unit 42 post (from page metadata) and the Check Point Dok page (approximate) should be confirmed.
No law-enforcement action, arrest or victim-loss total was found. Activity after 2019 was not found in the searches run.
Unclear whether all Retefe use is by one operator group or whether the malware is shared.
The Unit 42 Retefe post date (previously given as 2015-08) could not be confirmed; its content (Smoke Loader, UK targeting) suggests a later date, so the dated campaign entry was removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The relevant environment is consumer online banking and personal endpoints, including those of service members and families in or near Europe and Japan; DoD networks are not a stated target [S1][S7]. STEP 2: The actor adapts delivery and tooling over time (Tor to stunnel, new loaders, macOS port) and goes quiet between waves [S7]. STEP 3: Template is localized phishing, then certificate and proxy hijack, then OTP capture, with geo-fencing of victims [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued bank-customer fraud in European markets. MDCOA is the same tooling retargeted to additional countries or to personal devices of cleared personnel for credential theft; this is a judgment, not a sourced event. Candidate indicators: unexpected root certificates, changed DNS or proxy settings, PowerShell activity after Office document opens, unsigned or revoked-certificate macOS installers [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat as a criminal threat to personnel finances and personal devices, not a mission network threat, unless indicators appear on government systems. (2) Authorities: response is largely law-enforcement and bank-CERT led (for example Swiss MELANI engagement noted in 2014) [S2]; no military action implied. (3) Mission assurance: low direct impact; advise personnel on SMS-OTP weaknesses and certificate-store hygiene [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators through DC3 or civilian CERT channels if seen on DoD-adjacent devices.
